items.q: Group Anagrams — bucket strings by their character multiset
shortAnswer: Group strings that are anagrams of each other, keying each word by its character multiset.
Count each word's letters into a 26-int array and build a key from it; map each key to a bucket and return the buckets.
The canonical key is the decision: char counts cost O(k) per word and beat sorting at O(k log k). Total O(n·k).
items.prompt:
Given an array of strings, group the anagrams together: `["eat", "tea", "tan", "ate", "nat", "bat"]` → `[["eat","tea","ate"], ["tan","nat"], ["bat"]]`.

Two strings are anagrams when they have the same letters in different orders, so a sorted string or a character count is a canonical key. The interviewer is checking that you pick a cheap canonical form and explain the hashing cost honestly — a 26-int count vs sorting a string is a real trade-off at interview depth.
hints: Anagrams share a canonical form. What transformation turns "eat" and "tea" into the same key?
Sorting each string gives a canonical key but costs O(k log k) per word. Is there an O(k) key?
Use a `CharArray(26)` count and build the key from it — or `String(chars)` — so equal counts hash to equal keys. Map key → list, then return the lists.

code.caption: Char-count key, O(n·k) time / O(n·k) space

items.complexity: Time O(n·k) for the char-count key (n words of length k), or O(n·k log k) if you sort each word. Space O(n·k) for the output. The count-based key is strictly better than sorting and is what you should reach for first.
followUps: What if words are ASCII but not lowercase — do you still fit in 26 buckets?
How would you handle unicode (emoji, accented letters)? A `HashMap<Char, Int>` count, or normalize.
Return the groups in order of first appearance rather than hash order.

items.q: Container With Most Water — two pointers from opposite ends
shortAnswer: Find two vertical lines that, with the x-axis, enclose the most water — the maximum area.
Start pointers at both ends and move the shorter one inward; every pair skipped is provably worse because the shorter line caps the height.
The exchange argument is the question — moving the taller line only shrinks width while height stays capped. Time O(n), space O(1).
items.prompt:
Given `IntArray` heights where each entry is the height of a vertical line at that index, find the two lines that, together with the x-axis, hold the most water. Return the max area.

This is the canonical opposite-ends two-pointer problem. The insight that moving the shorter pointer is the *only* move worth making is the whole question — derive it out loud rather than guessing.
hints: Brute force is every pair: O(n²). Area = width × min(left, right). What makes a pair irrelevant?
Start pointers at both ends (max width). The area is bounded by the shorter line — moving the taller one in can only shrink or keep width while the height is still capped by the shorter one.
Move the pointer with the *smaller* height inward. Every pair you skip was provably worse, so a single pass finds the optimum.

code.caption: Shrink from both ends, O(n)

items.complexity: Time O(n) — each pointer moves at most n times. Space O(1). The brute force is O(n²) and is the wrong answer at this level unless you mention you're skipping it deliberately.
followUps: Why is it safe to skip the pairs when you move the shorter pointer? State the exchange argument.
What if heights are floats instead of ints?
Find the pair that maximizes area with the constraint that they must also both exceed some threshold.

items.q: Maximum sum of a subarray of size k — the fixed-size window template
shortAnswer: Return the maximum sum of any contiguous subarray of length exactly `k`.
Compute the first window's sum, then slide: add `arr[i]` and subtract `arr[i - k]` at each step, tracking the best.
The win is O(1) per step instead of re-summing `k` elements — O(n) total versus O(n·k), with O(1) space.
items.prompt:
Given an `IntArray` and a window size `k`, return the maximum sum of any contiguous subarray of length exactly `k`.

This is the warm-up that teaches the fixed-window pattern: advance the window by adding the new element and removing the outgoing one, so each step is O(1) instead of re-summing k elements.
hints: Re-summing every window costs O(n·k). What changes between two adjacent windows?
When the window slides right by one, exactly one element enters and one leaves.
Compute the first window's sum, then for each step add `arr[i]` and subtract `arr[i - k]`. Track the max.

code.caption: O(n) fixed-size window

items.complexity: Time O(n), space O(1). The naive re-sum is O(n·k) — always state the win when you reach for a window.
followUps: What if k can be larger than the array — how do you handle it?
Return the starting index of the max window, not just the sum.
What if the array has negative numbers — does the pattern change?

items.q: Longest substring with at most K distinct characters
shortAnswer: Find the length of the longest substring containing at most `k` distinct characters.
Grow the right edge, adding to a frequency map; while the distinct count exceeds `k`, shrink `left` until the invariant holds.
This shrinks on an invariant, not a schedule — the template for any 'at most' question. Each char moves once: O(n) time, O(k) space.
items.prompt:
Given a string and an integer `k`, return the length of the longest substring that contains at most `k` distinct characters.

Where the fixed window shrinks on a schedule, this one shrinks on an invariant: the window is valid only while the number of distinct chars is ≤ k. That makes it the template for every "at most" window question.
hints: A substring is contiguous — grow the right edge and track how many distinct chars are inside.
When a third distinct character arrives with k=2, the window is invalid. What must you do to the left edge?
Shrink `left` until the count of distinct characters drops back to k. A frequency map keyed by char lets you remove in O(1) per step.

code.caption: Variable window with a frequency map — O(n)

items.complexity: Time O(n) — each char enters and leaves the window once. Space O(k) for the frequency map.
followUps: Now require the substring to have *exactly* k distinct characters — what changes?
Longest substring with at most K *repeats* of any char — different invariant.
What if you must also return the substring itself?

items.q: Subarray Sum Equals K — count subarrays summing to a target
shortAnswer: Count contiguous subarrays whose sum equals a target `k`, in an array that may contain negatives.
A range sum is a difference of prefix sums: sweep, counting how many earlier prefixes equal `prefix - k`, seeded with `{0: 1}`.
The gotcha is negatives: a sliding window fails because sums aren't monotonic. Time O(n), space O(n) — contrast with O(n²) brute force.
items.prompt:
Given an `IntArray` (can contain negatives) and a target `k`, return the *number* of contiguous subarrays whose sum equals `k`.

Subarray sum is range sum, and range sum is a difference of prefix sums. The trick that separates juniors here: instead of checking every `(i, j)` pair of prefix sums, count how many earlier prefixes equal `prefix - k` as you sweep once. The presence of negatives means a sliding window does *not* work.
hints: Sum(arr[i..j]) = prefix[j] - prefix[i-1]. The problem becomes: count pairs of prefixes with the right difference.
A two-pointer window is invalid here because negatives mean sums are not monotonic — abandon that idea early and say why.
Sweep once, and at each prefix, ask: how many previous prefixes equal `prefix - k`? Keep a `HashMap<Int, Int>` of prefix-sum → count, seeded with `{0: 1}`.

code.caption: One pass with a prefix-count map — O(n)

items.complexity: Time O(n), space O(n). The O(n²) brute force enumerates all ranges — always contrast with it explicitly.
followUps: Why does seeding `{0: 1}` matter? Trace a subarray that starts at index 0.
Count subarrays whose sum is divisible by k — how does the map key change?
Find the *longest* subarray with sum k — what do you store in the map then?

items.pattern: Binary search on a sorted array
items.q: Search in a Rotated Sorted Array
shortAnswer: Search a rotated sorted array for a target, returning its index or -1, in O(log n).
Binary search, but first decide which half is sorted via `nums[lo] <= nums[mid]`, then test whether the target lies within that run's bounds.
Say 'one side is sorted, check its bounds, else go the other way'. Duplicates can degrade the worst case to O(n).
items.prompt:
Given a sorted array that has been rotated at an unknown pivot (e.g. `[4,5,6,7,0,1,2]`) and a target, return its index or -1. Values are distinct.

`O(n)` linear search is trivial; the whole point is the binary search. The classic trap: after `mid`, *one* half is always fully sorted — decide which, and whether the target can be in it. Say "one side is sorted, check whether the target is inside its bounds, else go the other way" and you own the problem.
hints: Even rotated, the array is two sorted runs. After splitting at `mid`, at least one run is fully sorted.
Check `arr[lo] <= arr[mid]` to identify the left run as sorted; else the right run is the sorted one.
If the sorted run contains the target by its bounds, search inside it; otherwise discard it and search the other run.

code.caption: Find the sorted half each step — O(log n)

items.complexity: Time O(log n), space O(1). Mention the duplicate case: with repeats you may have to drop the `<=` optimization to linear-ish in the worst case.
followUps: Find the index of the rotation pivot in O(log n).
What breaks when the array contains duplicates? Worst case becomes O(n) — why?
Search for the minimum element in a rotated array.

items.q: Minimum Capacity to Ship Packages within D days
shortAnswer: Find the minimum ship capacity that ships packages in their given order within `D` days.
Binary search capacity from max weight to total weight, with a greedy `canShip` check that starts a new day when a package exceeds capacity.
Monotonicity is the signal to binary-search the answer; the greedy check must preserve package order. Time O(n log S), space O(1).
items.prompt:
Given `weights: IntArray` in order and a day limit `D`, find the minimum ship capacity such that the packages can be shipped in the order they appear, splitting them across `D` consecutive days.

This is the canonical "binary search on the answer" problem: the answer (capacity) is monotonic — if C works, C+1 works. You binary-search the capacity and run a greedy feasibility check (`canShip`) at each candidate.
hints: There is no way to guess the capacity directly. But is the predicate "capacity C is feasible" monotonic in C?
Yes — if C works, any larger capacity works. That monotonicity is the signal to binary-search the answer space [max(weights) .. sum(weights)].
At each candidate C, simulate loading day by day in order; if a day would exceed C, start a new day. Feasible iff days used ≤ D. Binary search the smallest feasible C.

code.caption: Binary search on the answer — O(n log S)

items.complexity: Time O(n log S) where S = sum(weights) — log S candidates, each checked in O(n). Space O(1). The greedy check inside is the part interviewers probe: it must preserve package order.
followUps: Why must packages ship in order? What would change if they could be reordered?
Now minimize the maximum *weight carried on a single day* instead of capacity — identical answer space.
Koko eating bananas is the same pattern — name the shared skeleton.
